In the code chunk below, read_csv() of readr is used to import WHData-2018.csv into R and parsed it into tibble R data frame format.

wh <- read_csv("data/WHData-2018.csv")

The output tibbled data frame is called wh.



Next, we need to change the rows by country name instead of row number by using the code chunk below.

row.names(wh) <- wh$Country

Notice that the row number has been replaced into the country name.



The data was loaded into a data frame, but it has to be a data matrix to make your heatmap.
The code chunk below will be used to transform wh data frame into a data matrix.

wh1 <- dplyr::select(wh, c(3, 7:12))
wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh)

Notice that wh_matrix is in R matrix format.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 3
text:
There are many R packages and functions can be used to drawing static heatmaps, they are:

heatmap()of R stats package. It draws a simple heatmap.
heatmap.2() of gplots R package. It draws an enhanced heatmap compared to the R base function.
pheatmap() of pheatmap R package. pheatmap package also known as Pretty Heatmap. The package provides functions to draws pretty heatmaps and provides more control to change the appearance of heatmaps.
ComplexHeatmap package of R/Bioconductor package. The package draws, annotates and arranges complex heatmaps (very useful for genomic data analysis). The full reference guide of the package is available here.
superheat package: A Graphical Tool for Exploring Complex Datasets Using Heatmaps. A system for generating extendable and customizable heatmaps for exploring complex datasets, including big data and data with multiple data types. The full reference guide of the package is available here.

In this section, you will learn how to plot static heatmaps by using heatmap() of R Stats package.


In this sub-section, we will plot a heatmap by using heatmap() of Base Stats. The code chunk is given below.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv=NA, Colv=NA)








Note:

By default, heatmap() plots a cluster heatmap. The arguments Rowv=NA and Colv=NA are used to switch off the option of plotting the row and column dendrograms.

To plot a cluster heatmap, we just have to use the default as shown in the code chunk below.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix)








Note:

The order of both rows and columns is different compare to the native wh_matrix. This is because heatmap do a reordering using clusterisation: it calculates the distance between each pair of rows and columns and try to order them by similarity. Moreover, the corresponding dendrogram are provided beside the heatmap.

Here, red cells denotes small values, and red small ones. This heatmap is not really informative. Indeed, the Happiness Score variable have relatively higher values, what makes that the other variables with small values all look the same. Thus, we need to normalize this matrix. This is done using the scale argument. It can be applied to rows or to columns following your needs.
The code chunk below normalises the matrix column-wise.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale="column",
                      cexRow = 0.6, 
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))








Notice that the values are scaled now. Also note that margins argument is used to ensure that the entire x-axis labels are displayed completely and, cexRow and cexCol arguments are used to define the font size used for y-axis and x-axis labels respectively.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 3
text:
heatmaply is an R package for building interactive cluster heatmap that can be shared online as a stand-alone HTML file. It is designed and maintained by Tal Galili.
Before we get started, you should review the Introduction to Heatmaply to have an overall understanding of the features and functions of Heatmaply package. You are also required to have the user manualof the package handy with you for reference purposes.
In this section, you will gain hands-on experience on using heatmaply to design an interactive cluster heatmap. We will still use the wh_matrix as the input data.



heatmaply(mtcars)





The code chunk below shows the basic syntax needed to create n interactive heatmap by using heatmaply package.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])





Note that:

Different from heatmap(), for heatmaply() the default horizontal dendrogram is placed on the left hand side of the heatmap.
The text label of each raw, on the other hand, is placed on the right hand side of the heat map.
When the x-axis marker labels are too long, they will be rotated by 135 degree from the north.




When analysing multivariate data set, it is very common that the variables in the data sets includes values that reflect different types of measurement. In general, these variables’ values have their own range. In order to ensure that all the variables have comparable values, data transformation are commonly used before clustering.
Three main data transformation methods are supported by heatmaply(), namely: scale, normalise and percentilse.



When all variables are came from or assumed to come from some normal distribution, then scaling (i.e.: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation) would bring them all close to the standard normal distribution.
In such a case, each value would reflect the distance from the mean in units of standard deviation.
The scale argument in heatmaply() supports column and row scaling.

The code chunk below is used to scale variable values columewise.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")









When variables in the data comes from possibly different (and non-normal) distributions, the normalize function can be used to bring data to the 0 to 1 scale by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the maximum of all observations.
This preserves the shape of each variable’s distribution while making them easily comparable on the same “scale”.

Different from Scaling, the normalise method is performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))









This is similar to ranking the variables, but instead of keeping the rank values, divide them by the maximal rank.
This is done by using the ecdf of the variables on their own values, bringing each value to its empirical percentile.
The benefit of the percentize function is that each value has a relatively clear interpretation, it is the percent of observations that got that value or below it.

Similar to Normalize method, the Percentize method is also performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))









heatmaply supports a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithm. The main arguments provided are:

distfun: function used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between both rows and columns. Defaults to dist. The options “pearson”, “spearman” and “kendall” can be used to use correlation-based clustering, which uses as.dist(1 - cor(t(x))) as the distance metric (using the specified correlation method).
hclustfun: function used to compute the hierarchical clustering when Rowv or Colv are not dendrograms. Defaults to hclust.
dist_method default is NULL, which results in “euclidean” to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to distfun. By default distfun is “dist”” hence this can be one of “euclidean”, “maximum”, “manhattan”, “canberra”, “binary” or “minkowski”.
hclust_method default is NULL, which results in “complete” method to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to hclustfun. By default hclustfun is hclust hence this can be one of “ward.D”, “ward.D2”, “single”, “complete”, “average” (= UPGMA), “mcquitty” (= WPGMA), “median” (= WPGMC) or “centroid” (= UPGMC).

In general, a clustering model can be calibrated either manually or statistically.



In the code chunk below, the heatmap is plotted by using hierachical clustering algorithm with “Euclidean distance” and “ward.D” method.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")








In order to determine the best clustering method and number of cluster the dend_expend() and find_k() functions of dendextend package will be used.

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6137851
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6289186
3      unknown         single 0.4774362
4      unknown       complete 0.6434009
5      unknown        average 0.6701688
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.5020102
7      unknown         median 0.5901833
8      unknown       centroid 0.6338734


First, the dend_expend() will be used to determine the recommended clustering method to be used.
The output table shows that “average” method should be used because it gave the high optimum value.
Next, find_k() is used to determine the optimal number of cluster.

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)








Figure above shows that k=3 would be good.
With reference to the statistical analysis results, we can prepare the code chunk as shown below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)








One of the problems with hierarchical clustering is that it doesn’t actually place the rows in a definite order, it merely constrains the space of possible orderings. Take three items A, B and C. If you ignore reflections, there are three possible orderings: ABC, ACB, BAC. If clustering them gives you ((A+B)+C) as a tree, you know that C can’t end up between A and B, but it doesn’t tell you which way to flip the A+B cluster. It doesn’t tell you if the ABC ordering will lead to a clearer-looking heatmap than the BAC ordering.
heatmaply uses the seriation package to find an optimal ordering of rows and columns. Optimal means to optimize the Hamiltonian path length that is restricted by the dendrogram structure. This, in other words, means to rotate the branches so that the sum of distances between each adjacent leaf (label) will be minimized. This is related to a restricted version of the travelling salesman problem.
Here we meet our first seriation algorithm: Optimal Leaf Ordering (OLO). This algorithm starts with the output of an agglomerative clustering algorithm and produces a unique ordering, one that flips the various branches of the dendrogram around so as to minimize the sum of dissimilarities between adjacent leaves. Here is the result of applying Optimal Leaf Ordering to the same clustering result as the heatmap above.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")





The default options is “OLO” (Optimal leaf ordering) which optimizes the above criterion (in O(n^4)). Another option is “GW” (Gruvaeus and Wainer) which aims for the same goal but uses a potentially faster heuristic.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "GW")





The option “mean” gives the output we would get by default from heatmap functions in other packages such as gplots::heatmap.2.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "mean")





The option “none” gives us the dendrograms without any rotation that is based on the data matrix.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none")








The default colour palette uses by heatmaply is viridis. heatmaply users, however, can use other colour palettes in order to improve the aestheticness and visual friendliness of the heatmap.
In the code chunk below, the Blues colour palette of rColorBrewer is used.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues)








Beside providing a wide collection of arguments for meeting the statistical analysis needs, heatmaply also provides many plotting features to ensure cartographic quality heatmap can be produced.
In the code chunk below the following arguments are used:

k_row is used to produce 5 groups.
margins is used to change the top margin to 60 and row margin to 200.
fontsizw_row and fontsize_col are used to change the font size for row and column labels to 4.
main is used to write the main title of the plot.
xlab and ylab are used to write the x-axis and y-axis labels respectively.


heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          Colv=NA,
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 5,
          margins = c(NA,200,60,NA),
          fontsize_row = 3,
          fontsize_col = 7,
          main="World Happiness Score and Variables by Country, 2018 \nDataTransformation using Normalise Method",
          xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
          ylab = "World Countries"
          )

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 4
text:
Parallel coordinates plot is a data visualisation specially designed for visualising and analysing multivariate, numerical data. It is ideal for comparing multiple variables together and seeing the relationships between them. For example, the variables contribute to Happiness Index. Parallel coordinates was invented by Alfred Inselberg in the 1970s as a way to visualize high-dimensional data. This data visualisation technique is more often found in academic and scientific communities than in business and consumer data visualizations. As pointed out by Stephen Few(2006), “This certainly isn’t a chart that you would present to the board of directors or place on your Web site for the general public. In fact, the strength of parallel coordinates isn’t in their ability to communicate some truth in the data to others, but rather in their ability to bring meaningful multivariate patterns and comparisons to light when used interactively for analysis.” For example, parallel coordinates plot can be used to characterise clusters detected during customer segmentation.
By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experience on:

plotting statistic parallel coordinates plots by using ggparcoord() of GGally package, and
plotting interactive parallel coordinates plots by using parallelPlot package.




For this exercise, the GGally, parallelPlot and tidyverse packages will be used.
The code chunks below are used to install and load the packages in R.

pacman::p_load(GGally, parallelPlot, tidyverse)




In the code chunk below, read_csv() of readr package is used to import WHData-2018.csv into R and save it into a tibble data frame object called wh.

wh <- read_csv("data/WHData-2018.csv")




In this section, you will learn how to plot static parallel coordinates plot by using ggparcoord() of GGally package. Before getting started, it is a good practice to read the function description in detail.


Code chunk below shows a typical syntax used to plot a basic static parallel coordinates plot by using ggparcoord().

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12))








Notice that only two argument namely data and columns is used. Data argument is used to map the data object (i.e. wh) and columns is used to select the columns for preparing the parallel coordinates plot.



The basic parallel coordinates failed to reveal any meaning understanding of the World Happiness measures. In this section, you will learn how to makeover the plot by using a collection of arguments provided by ggparcoord().

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happines Variables"
) +
theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1,
    size = 8
  )
)








Things to learn from the code chunk above.

groupColumn argument is used to group the observations (i.e. parallel lines) by using a single variable (i.e. Region) and colour the parallel coordinates lines by region name.
scale argument is used to scale the variables in the parallel coordinate plot by using uniminmax method. The method univariately scale each variable so the minimum of the variable is zero and the maximum is one.
alphaLines argument is used to reduce the intensity of the line colour to 0.2. The permissible value range is between 0 to 1.
boxplot argument is used to turn on the boxplot by using logical TRUE. The default is FALSE.
title argument is used to provide the parallel coordinates plot a title.




Since ggparcoord() is developed by extending ggplot2 package, we can combination use some of the ggplot2 function when plotting a parallel coordinates plot.
In the code chunk below, facet_wrap() of ggplot2 is used to plot 10 small multiple parallel coordinates plots. Each plot represent one geographical region such as East Asia.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)








One of the aesthetic defect of the current design is that some of the variable names overlap on x-axis.



To make the x-axis text label easy to read, let us rotate the labels by 30 degrees. We can rotate axis text labels using theme() function in ggplot2 as shown in the code chunk below.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

To rotate x-axis text labels, we use axis.text.x as argument to theme() function. And we specify element_text(angle = 30) to rotate the x-axis text by an angle 30 degree.




Rotating x-axis text labels to 30 degrees makes the label overlap with the plot and we can avoid this by adjusting the text location using hjust argument to theme’s text element with element_text(). We use axis.text.x as we want to change the look of x-axis text.

ggparcoord(data = wh, 
           columns = c(7:12), 
           groupColumn = 2,
           scale = "uniminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happines Variables by Region") +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust=1))











Further adjustments to the plot

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.2,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of World Happiness Variables by Region"
) +
facet_wrap(~ Region, scales = "free_x") +
theme(
  axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 60,
    hjust = 1,
    size = 10
  ),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 10),
  plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.position = "bottom"
)












parallelPlot is an R package specially designed to plot a parallel coordinates plot by using ‘htmlwidgets’ package and d3.js. In this section, you will learn how to use functions provided in parallelPlot package to build interactive parallel coordinates plot.


The code chunk below plot an interactive parallel coordinates plot by using parallelPlot().

wh <- wh %>%
  select("Happiness score", c(7:12))
parallelPlot(wh,
             width = 320,
             height = 250)





Notice that some of the axis labels are too long. You will learn how to overcome this problem in the next step.



In the code chunk below, rotateTitle argument is used to avoid overlapping axis labels.

parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE)





One of the useful interactive feature of parallelPlot is we can click on a variable of interest, for example Happiness score, the monotonous blue colour (default) will change a blue with different intensity colour scheme will be used.



We can change the default blue colour scheme by using continousCS argument as shown in the code chunk below.

parallelPlot(wh,
             continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
             rotateTitle = TRUE)








In the code chunk below, histoVisibility argument is used to plot histogram along the axis of each variables.

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh))
parallelPlot(wh,
             rotateTitle = TRUE,
             histoVisibility = histoVisibility)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 5
text:
By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will be able to:

Transform transaction data into a treemap-compatible structure using functions from the dplyr package
Prepare and manipulate hierarchical data for treemap visualisation
Create static treemap visualisations using the treemap package
Design interactive treemap visualisations using the d3treeR package




Before we get started, you are required to check if treemap and tidyverse pacakges have been installed in you R.

pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse) 




In this exercise, REALIS2018.csv data will be used. This dataset provides information of private property transaction records in 2018. The dataset is extracted from REALIS portal (https://spring.ura.gov.sg/lad/ore/login/index.cfm) of Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).


In the code chunk below, read_csv() of readr is used to import realis2018.csv into R and parsed it into tibble R data.frame format.

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv") 

The output tibble data.frame is called realis2018.



The data.frame realis2018 is in trasaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not appropriate to be used to plot a treemap. In this section, we will perform the following steps to manipulate and prepare a data.frtame that is appropriate for treemap visualisation:

group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale, and
compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics on No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm) and Transacted Price ($) respectively.

Two key verbs of dplyr package, namely: group_by() and summarize() will be used to perform these steps.
group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retained.
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x). They are described in detail in vignette(“window-functions”).
sample_n() and sample_frac() sample the specified number/fraction of rows in each group.
summarise() computes the summary for each group.

In our case, group_by() will used together with summarise() to derive the summarised data.frame.



The code chank below shows a typical two lines code approach to perform the steps.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, 
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped,

                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),

                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

Note

The code chunk above is not very efficient because we have to give each intermediate data.frame a name, even though we don’t have to care about it.



The code chunk below shows a more efficient way to tackle the same processes by using the pipe, %>%:

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),

treemap package is a R package specially designed to offer great flexibility in drawing treemaps. The core function, namely: treemap() offers at least 43 arguments. In this section, we will only explore the major arguments for designing elegent and yet truthful treemaps.


In this section, treemap() of Treemap package is used to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total unit sold of resale condominium by geographic hierarchy in 2017.
First, we will select records belongs to resale condominium property type from realis2018_selected data frame.

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")




The code chunk below designed a treemap by using three core arguments of treemap(), namely: index, vSize and vColor.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the three arguments used:

index

The index vector must consist of at least two column names or else no hierarchy treemap will be plotted.
If multiple column names are provided, such as the code chunk above, the first name is the highest aggregation level, the second name the second highest aggregation level, and so on.

vSize

The column must not contain negative values. This is because it’s vaues will be used to map the sizes of the rectangles of the treemaps.


Warning:
The treemap above was wrongly coloured. For a correctly designed treemap, the colours of the rectagles should be in different intensity showing, in our case, median unit prices.
For treemap(), vColor is used in combination with the argument type to determines the colours of the rectangles. Without defining type, like the code chunk above, treemap() assumes type = index, in our case, the hierarchy of planning areas.



In the code chunk below, type argument is define as value.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above.

The rectangles are coloured with different intensity of green, reflecting their respective median unit prices.
The legend reveals that the values are binned into ten bins, i.e. 0-5000, 5000-10000, etc. with an equal interval of 5000.




There are two arguments that determine the mapping to color palettes: mapping and palette. The only difference between “value” and “manual” is the default value for mapping. The “value” treemap considers palette to be a diverging color palette (say ColorBrewer’s “RdYlBu”), and maps it in such a way that 0 corresponds to the middle color (typically white or yellow), -max(abs(values)) to the left-end color, and max(abs(values)), to the right-end color. The “manual” treemap simply maps min(values) to the left-end color, max(values) to the right-end color, and mean(range(values)) to the middle color.



The code chunk below shows a value type treemap.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

Although the colour palette used is RdYlBu but there are no red rectangles in the treemap above. This is because all the median unit prices are positive.
The reason why we see only 5000 to 45000 in the legend is because the range argument is by default c(min(values, max(values)) with some pretty rounding.




The “manual” type does not interpret the values as the “value” type does. Instead, the value range is mapped linearly to the colour palette.
The code chunk below shows a manual type treemap.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The colour scheme used is very confusing. This is because mapping = (min(values), mean(range(values)), max(values)). It is not wise to use diverging colour palette such as RdYlBu if the values are all positive or negative

To overcome this problem, a single colour palette such as Blues should be used.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











treemap() supports two popular treemap layouts, namely: “squarified” and “pivotSize”. The default is “pivotSize”.
The squarified treemap algorithm (Bruls et al., 2000) produces good aspect ratios, but ignores the sorting order of the rectangles (sortID). The ordered treemap, pivot-by-size, algorithm (Bederson et al., 2002) takes the sorting order (sortID) into account while aspect ratios are still acceptable.



The code chunk below plots a squarified treemap by changing the algorithm argument.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











When “pivotSize” algorithm is used, sortID argument can be used to dertemine the order in which the rectangles are placed from top left to bottom right.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )












treemapify is a R package specially developed to draw treemaps in ggplot2. In this section, you will learn how to designing treemps closely resemble treemaps designing in previous section by using treemapify. Before you getting started, you should read Introduction to “treemapify” its user guide.



ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`),
       layout = "scol",
       start = "bottomleft") + 
  geom_treemap() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "light blue", high = "blue")














TipObservations:




This treemap visualises property transaction data where the size of each rectangle represents the Total Unit Sold. Larger rectangles indicate higher sales volume.
The colour intensity represents the Median Unit Price ($ psm), with darker blue shades indicating higher property prices and lighter blue shades indicating lower
This visualisation helps identify patterns between transaction volume and pricing, highlighting which property segments are more actively traded and which command premium prices.






Group by Planning Region

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`),
       start = "topleft") + 
  geom_treemap()














TipObservations:




This treemap groups property transactions by Planning Region, where the size of each rectangle represents the Total Unit Sold. Larger blocks indicate regions or developments with higher transaction volumes.
The colour intensity reflects the Median Unit Price ($ psm), with lighter blue shades indicating higher-priced properties and darker blue shades representing relatively lower-priced properties.
This visualisation highlights differences in both transaction activity and pricing across planning regions, allowing easier identification of regions with strong sales activity and premium property values.



Group by Planning Area

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) + 
  geom_treemap()














TipObservations:




This treemap visualises property transactions grouped by both Planning Region and Planning Area, providing a more detailed hierarchical view of the housing market structure.
Compared to the previous treemap grouped only by Planning Region, this visualisation introduces an additional grouping by Planning Area, providing a more detailed hierarchical view of transaction volume and pricing differences within each region.
This allows for finer comparison of local property market patterns and identification of high-value planning areas.



Adding boundary line

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected, 
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) + 
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40",
                                size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20")














TipObservations:




The addition of subgroup boundary lines improves the separation between regions and planning areas, making the hierarchical structure and clustering patterns easier to distinguish visually.
Compared to the previous treemap, this version provides clearer visual organisation and readability by introducing explicit borders between groups.
This enhances interpretation of regional transaction patterns and pricing differences while reducing visual clutter between adjacent areas.

In the code chunk below, read_csv() of readr is used to import realis2018.csv into R and parsed it into tibble R data.frame format.

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv") 

The output tibble data.frame is called realis2018.

group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale, and

group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retained.
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x). They are described in detail in vignette(“window-functions”).

                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),

Improvements made:

Added descriptive chart title



Applied colour-coded axis labels for clarity



Enhanced distinction between Young, Active, and Old population groups
Clearer description in the tooltip



View Code
label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt, x = 0.1, y = 1, ax = 0, ay = 0,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper", align = "center",
    font       = list(family = "serif", size = 15, color = "white"),
    bgcolor    = "#b3b3b3",
    bordercolor = "black",
    borderwidth = 2
  )
}

axis <- function(txt, col) {
  list(
    title    = list(text = txt, font = list(color = col)),
    tickformat = ".0%",
    tickfont = list(size = 10, color = col),
    linecolor = col                 # axis line
  )
}

  aaxis = axis("Young" , "#0033A0"),   # red
  baxis = axis("Active", "#86110D"),   # green
  caxis = axis("Old"   , "#1C6B17")    # blue
)

plot_ly(
  agpop_mutated,
  a    = ~YOUNG,
  b    = ~ACTIVE,
  c    = ~OLD,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  color = I("black"),

  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Young:  %{a:.0%}",
    "<br>Active: %{b:.0%}",
    "<br>Old:    %{c:.0%}",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) %>%
  layout(
    title       = list(text = "Population structure, 2015"),
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary     = ternaryAxes,

  )

corrplor() supports three layout types, namely: “full”, “upper” or “lower”. The default is “full” which display full matrix. The default setting can be changed by using the type argument of corrplot().

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower") 








The default layout of the corrgram can be further customised. For example, arguments diag and tl.col are used to turn off the diagonal cells and to change the axis text label colour to black colour respectively as shown in the code chunk and figure below.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         type="lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 Part 2
text:
Exploring the other layout design arguments

tl.cex & tl.srtcl.pos & cl.cex




Show the code
corrplot(
  wine.cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  type = "lower",
  diag = FALSE,
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.cex = 0.8,
  tl.srt = 45
)













Show the code
corrplot(
  wine.cor,
  method = "ellipse",
  type = "lower",
  diag = FALSE,
  tl.col = "black",
  cl.pos = "r",
  cl.cex = 0.8
)











With corrplot package, it is possible to design corrgram with mixed visual matrix of one half and numerical matrix on the other half. In order to create a coorgram with mixed layout, the corrplot.mixed(), a wrapped function for mixed visualisation style will be used.
Figure below shows a mixed layout corrgram plotted using wine quality data.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black") 








The code chunk used to plot the corrgram are shown below.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black") 








Notice that argument lower and upper are used to define the visualisation method used. In this case ellipse is used to map the lower half of the corrgram and numerical matrix (i.e. number) is used to map the upper half of the corrgram. The argument tl.pos, on the other, is used to specify the placement of the axis label. Lastly, the diag argument is used to specify the glyph on the principal diagonal of the corrgram.



In statistical analysis, we are also interested to know which pair of variables their correlation coefficients are statistically significant.
Figure below shows a corrgram combined with the significant test. The corrgram reveals that not all correlation pairs are statistically significant. For example the correlation between total sulfur dioxide and free surfur dioxide is statistically significant at significant level of 0.1 but not the pair between total sulfur dioxide and citric acid.
With corrplot package, we can use the cor.mtest() to compute the p-values and confidence interval for each pair of variables.

wine.sig = cor.mtest(wine.cor, conf.level= .95)

We can then use the p.mat argument of corrplot function as shown in the code chunk below.

corrplot(wine.cor,
         method = "number",
         type = "lower",
         diag = FALSE,
         tl.col = "black",
         tl.srt = 45,
         p.mat = wine.sig$p,
         sig.level = .05) 











Matrix reorder is very important for mining the hiden structure and pattern in a corrgram. By default, the order of attributes of a corrgram is sorted according to the correlation matrix (i.e. “original”). The default setting can be over-write by using the order argument of corrplot(). Currently, corrplot package support four sorting methods, they are:

“AOE” is for the angular order of the eigenvectors. See Michael Friendly (2002) for details.
“FPC” for the first principal component order.
“hclust” for hierarchical clustering order, and “hclust.method” for the agglomeration method to be used.

“hclust.method” should be one of “ward”, “single”, “complete”, “average”, “mcquitty”, “median” or “centroid”.

“alphabet” for alphabetical order.

“AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet”. More algorithms can be found in seriation package.

corrplot.mixed(wine.cor, 
               lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               order="AOE",
               tl.col = "black") 











If using hclust, corrplot() can draw rectangles around the corrgram based on the results of hierarchical clustering.

corrplot(wine.cor, 
         method = "ellipse", 
         tl.pos = "lt",
         tl.col = "black",
         order="hclust",
         hclust.method = "ward.D",
         addrect = 3)

title: Take-Home Exercise 1 Technical Report
text:
Insurance companies often face challenges in identifying the underlying causes of poor profitability and high portfolio volatility. While traditional reporting tools provide summary-level insights, they may not fully reveal hidden patterns, risk drivers, or relationships within large and complex insurance datasets. As a result, insurers increasingly rely on visual analytics techniques to support more effective exploratory analysis and data-driven decision-making.
This assignment applies visual analytics methods to a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset using R programming and relevant visualisation libraries. Through the use of statistical graphics and interactive visualisations, the analysis aims to explore numerical, categorical, and temporal patterns within the portfolio. The study focuses on identifying key factors that may influence insurance profitability, claim behaviour, and portfolio volatility.
By leveraging visual analytics techniques such as distribution analysis, comparative visualisations, correlation analysis, and multivariate exploration, this investigation seeks to uncover meaningful insights that can support underwriting decisions, portfolio segmentation, and risk management strategies. Ultimately, this assignment demonstrates how visual analytics can enhance understanding of insurance data beyond conventional dashboard reporting approaches.



The dataset used in this assignment is a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio dataset containing policy-level information related to insurance coverage, claims experience, customer characteristics, and vehicle attributes. The dataset is intended to support exploratory visual analytics for identifying factors influencing portfolio profitability and volatility.
The data consists of both numerical and categorical variables collected across multiple insurance policies. Numerical variables include measures such as total premium, total incurred claims, total claims, total exposure, vehicle age, and driver age. These variables provide quantitative insights into policy performance, claims severity, and financial outcomes. Categorical variables include policy type, business type, fuel type, policy status, vehicle brand, and bonus score categories, which allow segmentation and comparative analysis across different customer and policy groups.




pacman::p_load(tidyverse, ggplot2, scales, ggdist, ggridges, ggstatsplot, DT, dplyr, treemapify, corrplot, GGally, factoextra) 






The motor insurance portfolio dataset was imported into R using the read_delim() function because the original CSV file used semicolon (;) delimiters instead of commas.

motor <- read_delim(
  "Assignment1/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv",
  delim = ";"
) 




Several pre-processing steps were performed to prepare the dataset for visual analytics:

Converted categorical variables into factor data types
Checked for missing or invalid values
Standardised variable formats for analysis consistency


motor_clean <- motor %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))




To ensure the dataset was properly imported and transformed, preliminary validation and structure checking were performed using the glimpse() and summary() functions. These functions were used to inspect variable types, identify missing values, and review the overall distribution of numerical variables prior to visual analysis.
The glimpse() function provides an overview of the dataset structure, including variable names, data types, and sample observations, while the summary() function generates descriptive statistics such as minimum, maximum, mean, and quartile values for numerical variables.

Feature engineering was performed to derive additional analytical variables from the raw insurance dataset. These engineered features, including loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, underwriting profit, profitability group, driver age group, high risk indicator, provide more meaningful indicators for evaluating portfolio profitability, claims behaviour, and risk exposure.
Here is an explanation to the various derived variables:

Loss Ratio: calculated as total incurred claims divided by total premium, representing portfolio profitability.
Claim Frequency: calculated as total claims divided by total exposure, representing how often the claims occurred.
Claim Severity: calculated as total incurred claims divided by total claims, representing the average cost per claim.
Underwriting Profit: calculated as total premium minus total incurred claims, representing the profitability of individual policies.
Profitability Group: categorised based on loss ratio thresholds, representing whether a policy is profitable, moderately profitable, or loss-making from an underwriting perspective.
Driver Age Group: categorised based on driver age ranges, representing different customer demographic segments for analysing claim behaviour and risk exposure.
High Risk Indicator: derived based on policies with loss ratios greater than 1, representing policies where incurred claims exceed collected premiums and may indicate underwriting concern.


motor_clean <- motor_clean %>%
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = ifelse(total_premium > 0,
                        total_incurred / total_premium,
                        NA),

    claim_frequency = ifelse(total_exposure > 0,
                             total_claims / total_exposure,
                             NA),

    claim_severity = ifelse(total_claims > 0,
                            total_incurred / total_claims,
                            NA),

    underwriting_profit =
      total_premium - total_incurred
  ) 


motor_clean <- motor_clean %>%
  mutate(

    # Profitability Group
    profitability_group = case_when(
      loss_ratio < 0.6 ~ "Profitable",
      loss_ratio < 1 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Loss Making"
    ),

    # Driver Age Group
    driver_age_group = case_when(
      driver_age < 25 ~ "Young",
      driver_age < 60 ~ "Adult",
      TRUE ~ "Senior"
    ),

    # High Risk Indicator
    high_risk = ifelse(
      loss_ratio > 1,
      "High Risk",
      "Normal"
    )

  ) 





Univariate visual analysis was conducted to examine the individual distribution and characteristics of numerical and categorical variables within the motor insurance portfolio dataset. This analysis helps identify data patterns, concentration, skewness, outliers, and segment composition prior to performing more advanced multivariate analysis.






View Code
ggplot(motor_clean, aes(x = "", y = total_premium)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Total Premium",
    x = "",
    y = "Total Premium"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()















TipObservations:




The violin-boxplot of total premium shows that the distribution is positively skewed, where the majority of insurance policies are concentrated within the lower premium range. The widest section of the violin plot appears around the lower-to-middle premium values, indicating that most policyholders pay relatively moderate premiums. The median premium, represented by the line inside the boxplot, is also positioned within the lower range of the distribution.
The long upper tail and numerous outlier points suggest that a smaller number of policies have substantially higher premium values. These high-premium policies may represent higher-risk customers, larger coverage amounts, or specialised insurance products that require greater premium charges. The presence of extreme premium outliers indicates variability within the insurance portfolio and highlights the insurer’s exposure to different customer risk segments.








View Code
# Log-transformed histogram
ggplot(motor_clean, aes(x = "", y = total_incurred)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white", outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Total Incurred Claims",
    x = "",
    y = "Total Incurred Claims"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()















TipObservations:




The violin-boxplot of total incurred claims shows that the distribution is heavily concentrated near lower claims values, indicating that most insurance policies incur relatively small claim amounts. The narrow lower section and compressed boxplot near the bottom suggest that a large proportion of policyholders either make small claims or experience minimal incurred losses.
The distribution also exhibits a long upper tail with numerous extreme outliers extending beyond 5,000. This indicates that a relatively small number of policies generate exceptionally large claims, contributing disproportionately to portfolio volatility and underwriting risk. Such positively skewed claim distributions are commonly observed in insurance portfolios where rare but severe claim events significantly impact profitability.

  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Density Plot of Loss Ratio",
    x = "Loss Ratio",

  ) +

The regression results confirmed that total incurred claims, loss ratio, claim frequency, and claim severity are statistically significant predictors of underwriting profit, with all variables demonstrating strong significance levels. In particular, total incurred claims and loss ratio exhibited the strongest negative impact on profitability, reinforcing the conclusion that claims-related factors are the primary drivers of underwriting volatility and financial performance.
The use of visual analytics techniques including heatmaps, treemaps, correlation analysis, pairwise relationship plots, clustering, and regression analysis enabled the identification of hidden relationships and high-risk portfolio segments that may not be easily observable through traditional reporting methods. These insights may support insurers in improving underwriting strategy, pricing optimisation, risk segmentation, and claims management practices, ultimately contributing to more sustainable portfolio profitability and enhanced risk management decisions.

Feature engineering was performed to derive additional analytical variables from the raw insurance dataset. These engineered features, including loss ratio, claim frequency, claim severity, underwriting profit, profitability group, driver age group, high risk indicator, provide more meaningful indicators for evaluating portfolio profitability, claims behaviour, and risk exposure.
Here is an explanation to the various derived variables:

Loss Ratio: calculated as total incurred claims divided by total premium, representing portfolio profitability.
Claim Frequency: calculated as total claims divided by total exposure, representing how often the claims occurred.
Claim Severity: calculated as total incurred claims divided by total claims, representing the average cost per claim.
Underwriting Profit: calculated as total premium minus total incurred claims, representing the profitability of individual policies.
Profitability Group: categorised based on loss ratio thresholds, representing whether a policy is profitable, moderately profitable, or loss-making from an underwriting perspective.
Driver Age Group: categorised based on driver age ranges, representing different customer demographic segments for analysing claim behaviour and risk exposure.
High Risk Indicator: derived based on policies with loss ratios greater than 1, representing policies where incurred claims exceed collected premiums and may indicate underwriting concern.


motor_clean <- motor_clean %>%
  mutate(
    loss_ratio = ifelse(total_premium > 0,
                        total_incurred / total_premium,
                        NA),

    claim_frequency = ifelse(total_exposure > 0,
                             total_claims / total_exposure,
                             NA),

    claim_severity = ifelse(total_claims > 0,
                            total_incurred / total_claims,
                            NA),

    underwriting_profit =
      total_premium - total_incurred
  ) 


motor_clean <- motor_clean %>%
  mutate(

    # Profitability Group
    profitability_group = case_when(
      loss_ratio < 0.6 ~ "Profitable",
      loss_ratio < 1 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Loss Making"
    ),

    # Driver Age Group
    driver_age_group = case_when(
      driver_age < 25 ~ "Young",
      driver_age < 60 ~ "Adult",
      TRUE ~ "Senior"
    ),

    # High Risk Indicator
    high_risk = ifelse(
      loss_ratio > 1,
      "High Risk",
      "Normal"
    )

  )

title: Take-Home Exercise 1 Technical Report
text:
Bivariate visual analysis was conducted to examine the relationships and interactions between key variables within the motor insurance portfolio dataset in order to identify factors influencing profitability and claims volatility. Through the use of comparative and relationship-based visual analytics techniques, the analysis explores how variables such as policy type, business type, claim severity, loss ratio, and risk category are associated with underwriting performance and portfolio risk exposure. This helps uncover hidden patterns, segment differences, correlations, and high-risk areas that support more effective underwriting, pricing, and risk management decisions.




View Code
ggplot(motor_clean,
       aes(x = driver_age_group,
           y = claim_severity,
           fill = driver_age_group)) +

  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +

  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.1,
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    fill = "white"
  ) +

  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5000)) +

  labs(
    title = "Claim Severity by Driver Age Group",
    subtitle =
      "Comparison of average claim costs across driver age segments",
    x = "Driver Age Group",
    y = "Claim Severity"
  ) +

  theme_minimal() +

  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )















TipObservations:




The violin plot reveals that claim severity distributions differ across driver age groups, although all groups exhibit substantial variability and a strong right-skewed distribution. Most claim severity values are concentrated at lower to moderate claim amounts, as shown by the wider portions near the lower range of the violins, while the long upper tails indicate the presence of relatively rare but extremely costly claims.
Among the three groups, senior drivers appear to have a slightly higher median claim severity and a broader spread in the interquartile range, suggesting greater volatility and potentially higher financial risk exposure. Young drivers also demonstrate considerable variability with several high-cost outliers, while adult drivers show comparatively more stable claim severity distributions. Overall, the analysis suggests that driver age may influence claim cost behaviour and should be considered in underwriting, pricing, and risk segmentation strategies.








View Code
ggplot(motor_clean,
       aes(x = total_premium,
           y = total_incurred)) +

  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.2,
    color = "lightblue"
  ) +

  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "red"
  ) +

  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 3000),
    ylim = c(0, 5000)
  ) +

  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +

    subtitle =
      "Relationship between premium collected and claims incurred",
    x = "Total Premium",
    y = "Total Incurred Claims"
  ) +

  theme_minimal()















TipObservations:




The scatter plot indicates a positive relationship between total premium collected and total incurred claims, as shown by the upward-sloping regression line. This suggests that policies with higher premiums generally tend to be associated with higher claim amounts, which is reasonable as higher-risk policies are often priced with larger premiums to compensate for greater expected losses.
However, the data points are widely dispersed around the regression line, indicating substantial variability in claim outcomes even among policies with similar premium levels. A large concentration of observations appears near the lower premium range, while several extreme claim outliers are observed across different premium levels, highlighting the presence of high-cost claim events and underwriting volatility within the portfolio. The weak clustering around the trend line suggests that premium alone may not fully explain incurred claims, implying that additional factors such as driver profile, policy type, and risk exposure may also significantly influence claims behaviour.

“Where are the risky combinations?”


View Code
heatmap_data <- motor_clean %>%
  group_by(policy_type, business_type) %>%

TipObservations:




The heatmap reveals noticeable differences in average loss ratios across combinations of policy type and business type, indicating varying levels of underwriting profitability within the insurance portfolio. Darker colour intensities represent higher average loss ratios, suggesting segments where incurred claims are relatively high compared to collected premiums and where underwriting profitability may be weaker.
Among the policy categories, COMP_N under business type P exhibits the darkest colour intensity, indicating the highest average loss ratio and potentially the greatest underwriting risk exposure. In contrast, policy types such as TP and CC display lighter shades in certain business segments, suggesting comparatively lower average loss ratios and stronger profitability performance. The heatmap highlights how profitability can vary significantly across product and business combinations, demonstrating the importance of segment-specific pricing, underwriting controls, and portfolio monitoring strategies.






“Which business segments are largest, and are they profitable?”


View Code
treemap_data <- motor_clean %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  summarise(
    total_premium_sum = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_loss_ratio = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  treemap_data,
  aes(
    area = total_premium_sum,
    fill = avg_loss_ratio,
    label = policy_type
  )

  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",
    place = "centre",
    grow = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "lightblue",
    high = "darkred"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Treemap of Total Premium by Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Rectangle size represents total premium volume; colour represents average loss ratio",
    fill = "Avg Loss Ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()















TipObservations:




The treemap illustrates the distribution of total premium volume across different policy types, where larger rectangles represent policy categories contributing a greater share of premium revenue within the insurance portfolio. The CC and COMP_E policy types occupy the largest areas, indicating that these products dominate the portfolio in terms of premium generation and customer concentration. In contrast, policy types such as TP, TPG, and COMP_N contribute comparatively smaller premium volumes.
The colour intensity represents the average loss ratio associated with each policy type, providing insight into underwriting profitability alongside portfolio size. COMP_N displays the darkest red shade, indicating the highest average loss ratio and potentially the weakest underwriting profitability among the policy categories despite its relatively smaller premium contribution. Conversely, CC exhibits a lighter shade, suggesting comparatively lower average loss ratios and stronger underwriting performance. This combined visualisation highlights the importance of balancing portfolio growth with profitability, as high-premium segments do not necessarily correspond to high underwriting risk, while smaller segments may still contribute disproportionately to portfolio volatility.



While the heatmap focuses on identifying profitability patterns across combinations of policy type and business type, the treemap additionally incorporates portfolio size by representing premium volume through rectangle area. Together, these visualisations provide complementary insights into both underwriting performance and portfolio composition.
Overall Insights
The bivariate visual analysis revealed several important insights regarding the profitability and volatility of the motor insurance portfolio. Overall, the portfolio appears to remain largely profitable, as most policies fall within the profitable category and exhibit relatively low loss ratios. However, significant variability and underwriting volatility are still present across different policy segments, particularly within certain policy types and customer groups. The analysis also showed that claim severity distributions are highly right-skewed, indicating that while most claims are relatively moderate in value, a smaller number of extreme claims contribute disproportionately to portfolio risk exposure and financial uncertainty.
The heatmap and treemap analyses further highlighted that underwriting performance differs considerably across combinations of policy type and business type. Certain segments, such as COMP_N, demonstrated comparatively higher average loss ratios despite contributing smaller premium volumes, suggesting potential profitability concerns and elevated underwriting risk. Additionally, the scatterplot analysis showed only a weak-to-moderate relationship between premium collected and incurred claims, implying that premium alone may not fully explain claims behaviour and that other customer, policy, or risk-related variables may play important roles.
Based on these findings, several additional analyses can be conducted to further strengthen the investigation.

    )
  )(200)
)  















TipObservations:




The correlation heatmap highlights the strength and direction of relationships among key numerical variables within the insurance portfolio. A very strong positive correlation is observed between total_incurred and claim_severity (0.90), indicating that higher claim costs are closely associated with more severe claims. Similarly, total_incurred also shows a strong positive relationship with loss_ratio (0.68), suggesting that increased claims significantly reduce underwriting profitability.
Strong negative correlations are observed between underwriting_profit and both total_incurred (-1.00) and claim_severity (-0.90). This indicates that higher claims and more severe claim events directly reduce underwriting profits. In contrast, claim_frequency demonstrates relatively weak correlations with most variables, implying that claim severity has a greater financial impact on portfolio profitability than claim occurrence frequency alone.
Additionally, total_premium exhibits only weak relationships with most variables, suggesting that premium size alone may not be a strong predictor of claims behaviour or underwriting performance. Overall, the analysis identifies claim severity and incurred claims as the most influential drivers of portfolio risk and profitability.

ggpairs(pair_data)















TipObservations:




The pairwise relationship plot provides a comprehensive overview of the relationships among key numerical variables within the insurance portfolio, including total_premium, total_incurred, loss_ratio, claim_frequency, and claim_severity. The diagonal density plots indicate that most variables are heavily right-skewed, with the majority of observations concentrated at lower values and a small number of extreme outliers. This suggests that the portfolio contains many low-cost policies and claims, alongside a limited number of high-severity cases that contribute disproportionately to overall volatility.
Strong positive correlations are observed between total_incurred and claim_severity (0.813), as well as between total_incurred and loss_ratio (0.735), indicating that higher claims severity significantly increases incurred losses and reduces underwriting profitability. Loss_ratio also demonstrates moderate positive relationships with both claim_frequency and claim_severity, suggesting that both claim occurrence and claim size contribute to underwriting risk. In contrast, total_premium exhibits relatively weak correlations with the other variables, implying that premium size alone is not a strong predictor of claims behaviour or profitability outcomes. Overall, the analysis highlights claim severity and incurred claims as the primary drivers of portfolio risk exposure and underwriting performance.








View Code
set.seed(123)

cluster_data <- motor_clean %>%
  select(
    loss_ratio,
    claim_frequency,
    claim_severity,
    underwriting_profit
  ) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  sample_n(3000)

scaled_data <- scale(cluster_data)

kmeans_result <- kmeans(
  scaled_data,
  centers = 3,
  nstart = 25
)

fviz_cluster(
  kmeans_result,
  data = scaled_data,
  geom = "point",
  ellipse.type = "norm",
  palette = c(
    "#F4A6A6",   # soft pink
    "#63D28A",   # soft green
    "#7DA7F7"    # soft blue
  ),
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)















TipObservations:




The cluster analysis identifies three distinct groups of insurance policies based on underwriting profitability, claim severity, claim frequency, and loss ratio characteristics. Cluster 1 (pink) appears to represent the largest and most concentrated group, with observations located close to the centre of the plot. This suggests that the majority of policies exhibit relatively moderate claims behaviour and more stable underwriting performance.
Cluster 2 (green) is more widely dispersed and extends further along the positive Dim1 direction, indicating policies with greater variability and potentially higher-risk characteristics such as elevated claim severity, higher loss ratios, or reduced underwriting profitability. In contrast, Cluster 3 (blue) is separated along the negative Dim2 direction, suggesting another distinct policy segment with different claims behaviour and financial risk characteristics. Overall, the clear separation between clusters indicates that the insurance portfolio contains heterogeneous policy groups, highlighting opportunities for improved risk segmentation, pricing differentiation, and targeted underwriting strategies.

TipObservations:




The regression analysis indicates that all selected variables are statistically significant predictors of underwriting profit, as all p-values are below 0.001. Total incurred claims exhibit the strongest negative effect on underwriting profit, suggesting that higher claims costs substantially reduce portfolio profitability. Loss ratio also demonstrates a significant negative relationship, indicating that policies with higher claims relative to premiums contribute negatively to underwriting performance. Similarly, higher claim frequency and claim severity are associated with lower underwriting profit, confirming that both the occurrence and magnitude of claims influence portfolio volatility and profitability.
The model achieves an exceptionally high adjusted R-squared value of 0.9977, indicating that the selected variables explain nearly all variation in underwriting profit within the dataset. Overall, the findings statistically validate that claims-related variables, particularly total incurred claims and loss ratio, are the primary drivers of underwriting profitability and risk exposure in the insurance portfolio.



Overall Insights
The multivariate visual analytics revealed several important relationships influencing the profitability and volatility of the motor insurance portfolio. The correlation heatmap and pairwise relationship analysis showed that total incurred claims, claim severity, and loss ratio exhibit strong positive relationships, indicating that severe claim events are among the primary drivers of underwriting losses and portfolio volatility. In particular, claim severity demonstrated a strong negative relationship with underwriting profit, suggesting that a relatively small number of high-cost claims can significantly reduce portfolio profitability.
These findings were further statistically validated through regression analysis. The regression results confirmed that total incurred claims, loss ratio, claim frequency, and claim severity are all statistically significant predictors of underwriting profit, with p-values below 0.001. Among these variables, total incurred claims showed the strongest negative effect on profitability, while higher loss ratios and claim severity also substantially reduced underwriting performance. The exceptionally high adjusted R-squared value indicates that the selected risk variables explain a large proportion of variation in underwriting profit.
The heatmap and treemap analyses further highlighted that certain combinations of policy type and business type contribute disproportionately to underwriting risk. Policies under COMP_N and business type P recorded the highest average loss ratios, indicating weaker profitability performance within these segments. In contrast, CC and TP policies generally exhibited lower loss ratios and comparatively more stable underwriting outcomes.
The cluster analysis revealed that the insurance portfolio can be segmented into distinct customer risk groups based on variables such as premium size, incurred claims, claim severity, and loss ratio. While the majority of policies belong to relatively stable and profitable clusters, a smaller group of policies demonstrates substantially higher claims severity and underwriting volatility. These findings suggest that portfolio risk is concentrated within specific high-risk segments rather than being evenly distributed across all policies.
Overall, the analysis indicates that underwriting profitability is influenced not only by premium size, but also by the interaction between policy type, customer risk profile, claim severity, and claims behaviour. The results demonstrate the value of combining visual analytics with statistical validation techniques to uncover hidden risk concentrations and support more targeted underwriting, pricing, and portfolio management strategies.

title: Take-Home Exercise 1 Technical Report
text:
Based on the visual analytics findings, several strategies may help improve portfolio profitability and reduce underwriting volatility.


Policy segments such as COMP_N under business type P exhibited relatively high average loss ratios and may require closer underwriting review. The insurer could introduce stricter risk assessment criteria, tighter acceptance thresholds, or enhanced customer screening for these segments.



The strong relationship between incurred claims, claim severity, and underwriting losses suggests that certain high-risk policies may not be priced adequately relative to their expected claims exposure. Risk-based pricing models incorporating driver age, claims behaviour, and policy characteristics could help better align premiums with underlying risk levels.



Since severe claims contribute disproportionately to underwriting losses, the insurer should prioritise claim severity management through fraud detection, early claims intervention, repair cost controls, and enhanced claims investigation procedures. Reducing large claim events may significantly improve overall portfolio profitability.



The cluster analysis demonstrates that policyholders can be segmented into distinct behavioural and risk groups. Leveraging advanced segmentation techniques may allow the insurer to design more targeted underwriting, pricing, and retention strategies for different customer segments.



Although high-risk policies form a relatively small proportion of the portfolio, they contribute disproportionately to volatility and losses. Continuous monitoring using visual analytics dashboards and predictive models may help identify deteriorating risk segments earlier and support proactive risk mitigation decisions.

title: Take-Home Exercise 1 Technical Report
text:
This study demonstrates how visual analytics techniques can provide meaningful insights into the profitability and volatility of a motor insurance portfolio beyond conventional dashboard reporting. Through the application of univariate, bivariate, and multivariate visual analytics methods, the analysis successfully identified important patterns, relationships, and risk concentrations within the dataset.
The findings reveal that the portfolio is generally profitable overall, with most policies maintaining manageable loss ratios and stable underwriting performance. However, a smaller number of high-risk policies and severe claim events contribute disproportionately to underwriting volatility and financial losses. Variables such as claim severity, policy type, business type, and customer risk characteristics were found to significantly influence portfolio profitability.
These visual findings were further supported through statistical validation using regression analysis. The regression results confirmed that total incurred claims, loss ratio, claim frequency, and claim severity are statistically significant predictors of underwriting profit, with all variables demonstrating strong significance levels. In particular, total incurred claims and loss ratio exhibited the strongest negative impact on profitability, reinforcing the conclusion that claims-related factors are the primary drivers of underwriting volatility and financial performance.
The use of visual analytics techniques including heatmaps, treemaps, correlation analysis, pairwise relationship plots, clustering, and regression analysis enabled the identification of hidden relationships and high-risk portfolio segments that may not be easily observable through traditional reporting methods. These insights may support insurers in improving underwriting strategy, pricing optimisation, risk segmentation, and claims management practices, ultimately contributing to more sustainable portfolio profitability and enhanced risk management decisions.

📄 Introduction


Insurance companies frequently face difficulties identifying the root causes of underwriting losses and portfolio volatility. Traditional dashboard reporting often focuses on summary statistics and may fail to reveal deeper relationships hidden within complex insurance datasets. This study applies visual analytics techniques to explore customer behaviour, claims performance, underwriting profitability, and risk exposure within a motor insurance portfolio. The analysis aims to uncover meaningful patterns that may support pricing optimisation, underwriting decisions, and portfolio risk management.

📄 Data Wrangling


The dataset contains over 354,000 motor insurance policy records with variables related to premiums, claims, customer demographics, and vehicle characteristics. Several engineered variables were created to enhance the analytical value of the dataset. Loss ratio measures underwriting profitability, claim frequency measures claims occurrence rate, and claim severity measures average claim cost. Additional segmentation variables such as profitability group and high-risk indicator were also derived to support deeper portfolio analysis and underwriting evaluation.
